claim: P. aeruginosa infection activates caspase-11 in bone marrow-derived macrophage (BMDM) cells.
source: We found that activation of caspase-11 and cleavage of GSDMD in bone marrow-derived macrophage (BMDM) cells were not affected after incubation with P. aeruginosa and OMVs (Figure 1A, B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1A and quantification in Figure 1B showing caspase-11 activation.

claim: P. aeruginosa infection does not affect GSDMD cleavage in BMDM cells.
source: We found that activation of caspase-11 and cleavage of GSDMD in bone marrow-derived macrophage (BMDM) cells were not affected after incubation with P. aeruginosa and OMVs (Figure 1A, B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 1A and quantification in Figure 1B showing GSDMD cleavage.

claim: P. aeruginosa infection significantly inhibits caspase-1 activation in BMDM cells.
source: However, activation of caspase-1 was significantly inhibited in cells infected with P. aeruginosa (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 1A showing reduced caspase-1 activation.

claim: IL-1β secretion is diminished after P. aeruginosa infection in BMDM cells.
source: Consistent with the results of immunoblotting, the secretion of IL-1β was diminished after infection with P. aeruginosa (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data in Figure 1C showing reduced IL-1β levels.

claim: P. aeruginosa infection increases cell mortality rate in BMDM cells.
source: Although the mortality rate of P. aeruginosa-infected cells was increased (Figure 1D) and the survival rate was decreased (Figure 1E), there was not much difference compared to cells stimulated with intracellular E. coli.
evidence: Supported by LDH release assay data in Figure 1D.

claim: P. aeruginosa infection decreases cell survival rate in BMDM cells.
source: Although the mortality rate of P. aeruginosa-infected cells was increased (Figure 1D) and the survival rate was decreased (Figure 1E), there was not much difference compared to cells stimulated with intracellular E. coli.
evidence: Supported by ATP quantification assay data in Figure 1E.

claim: The activation of NLRP3 inflammasomes post non-canonical inflammasome stimulation is inhibited in the presence of P. aeruginosa.
source: These results indicate that the activation of NLRP3 inflammasomes post non-canonical inflammasome stimulation is inhibited in the presence of P. aeruginosa.
evidence: Inferred from the combined observations of normal caspase-11/GSDMD activation but inhibited caspase-1 activation and IL-1β secretion.

claim: P. aeruginosa infection results in normal caspase-4 activation in human macrophages.
source: Similar results were observed in human macrophage experiments, with normal caspase-4 activation and GSDMD cleavage after P. aeruginosa infection (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and quantification in 1B.

claim: P. aeruginosa infection results in normal GSDMD cleavage in human macrophages.
source: Similar results were observed in human macrophage experiments, with normal caspase-4 activation and GSDMD cleavage after P. aeruginosa infection (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and quantification in 1B.

claim: Caspase-1 activation is suppressed in human macrophages infected with P. aeruginosa.
source: However, the activation of caspase-1 was suppressed and IL-1β could not be secreted normally in these cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, C).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: IL-1β secretion is suppressed in human macrophages infected with P. aeruginosa.
source: However, the activation of caspase-1 was suppressed and IL-1β could not be secreted normally in these cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, C).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: GSDMD N-terminus can be normally localized on the mitochondrial membrane during P. aeruginosa infection.
source: The results indicate that GSDMD-N can be normally localized on the mitochondrial membrane (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by cellular component fractionation and immunoblotting data in Figure 1F.

claim: The release of mitochondrial DNA into the cytoplasm is not affected by P. aeruginosa infection.
source: In addition, the release of mitochondrial DNA into the cytoplasm was not affected by P. aeruginosa infection (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by PCR analysis data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The binding of NUR77 and NLRP3 is not affected during P. aeruginosa infection.
source: The binding of NUR77 and NLRP3 was not affected during the infection of P. aeruginosa (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The binding of NLRP3 to NEK7 is significantly inhibited during P. aeruginosa infection.
source: However, the binding of NLRP3 to NEK7 was significantly inhibited (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H.

claim: The inhibition of NLRP3 is potentially influenced by a certain inhibitory factor from P. aeruginosa.
source: These data suggest that the inhibition of NLRP3 is potentially influenced by a certain inhibitory factor from P. aeruginosa.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that NLRP3-NEK7 binding is inhibited while upstream signals remain intact.

claim: NLRP3 inflammasomes are activated after introducing LPS and mitochondrial DNA into Aim2 knockout macrophages.
source: We found that after introducing LPS and mitochondrial DNA, NLRP3 inflammasomes were activated (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 1G showing caspase-1 activation.

claim: NLRP3 activation is inhibited after incubation with P. aeruginosa in Aim2 knockout macrophages transfected with LPS and mitochondrial DNA.
source: However, NLRP3 activation was inhibited (Figure 1G) and the secretion of IL-1β was tremendously inhibited (Figure 1H) after incubation with P. aeruginosa.
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 1G.

claim: IL-1β secretion is tremendously inhibited after incubation with P. aeruginosa in Aim2 knockout macrophages transfected with LPS and mitochondrial DNA.
source: However, NLRP3 activation was inhibited (Figure 1G) and the secretion of IL-1β was tremendously inhibited (Figure 1H) after incubation with P. aeruginosa.
evidence: Supported by ELISA data in Figure 1H.

claim: GSDMD cleavage by caspase-11, rather than subsequent GSDMD cleavage by NLRP3, is the main factor causing cell death.
source: This was consistent with previous reports suggesting that GSDMD cleavage by caspase-11, rather than subsequent GSDMD cleavage by NLRP3, is the main factor causing cell death (Broz et al., 2020; Kayagaki et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Broz et al., 2020; Kayagaki et al., 2011).

claim: After Gsdmd knockout, the NLRP3 inflammasome becomes active when LPS and mitochondrial DNA are introduced into macrophages.
source: We found that after Gsdmd knockout, the NLRP3 inflammasome became active when LPS and mitochondrial DNA were introduced into macrophages.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental design and results described in the text.

claim: NLRP3 is still inhibited after incubation with P. aeruginosa in Gsdmd and Aim2 double knockout cells.
source: However, NLRP3 was still inhibited after incubation with P. aeruginosa (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1I.

claim: Potent inhibitory factors of P. aeruginosa may act upstream of GSDMD.
source: These results suggest that potent inhibitory factors of P. aeruginosa may act upstream of GSDMD.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that NLRP3 inhibition persists even in Gsdmd knockout cells.

claim: The activation of NLRP3 inflammasome is not affected after incubation with P. aeruginosa in Casp11 and Aim2 double knockout cells.
source: After incubation with P. aeruginosa, the activation of NLRP3 inflammasome was not affected (Figure 1K).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 1K.

claim: IL-1β secretion is no longer inhibited in Casp11 and Aim2 double knockout cells after P. aeruginosa incubation.
source: The secretion of IL-1β was no longer inhibited (Figure 1L).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data in Figure 1L.

claim: The inhibitory factors of P. aeruginosa require caspase-11 to take effect.
source: These data indicate that the inhibitory factors of P. aeruginosa requires caspase-11 to take effect.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that NLRP3 inhibition is relieved in Casp11 knockout cells.

claim: VgrG1a and VgrG2b repeatedly appeared in cells that met the screening criteria for caspase-11 substrates.
source: After sequencing, we found that VgrG1a and VgrG2b repeatedly appeared in cells that met the screening criteria.
evidence: Supported by the systematic screening system described and sequencing results.

claim: VgrG1a can be cleaved by mouse caspase-11.
source: We cloned the genes of VgrG1a and VgrG2b and cleaved them using mouse caspase-11. We found that they can both be cleaved (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: VgrG2b can be cleaved by mouse caspase-11.
source: We cloned the genes of VgrG1a and VgrG2b and cleaved them using mouse caspase-11. We found that they can both be cleaved (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 2B.

claim: VgrG1a can be cleaved by human caspase-4.
source: We also found that they can be cleaved by human caspase-4 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, Figure 2C), but not by caspase-11/4 mutants lacking enzymatic activities.
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: VgrG2b can be cleaved by human caspase-4.
source: We also found that they can be cleaved by human caspase-4 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, Figure 2C), but not by caspase-11/4 mutants lacking enzymatic activities.
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 2C.

claim: VgrG1a and VgrG2b cannot be cleaved by caspase-11/4 mutants lacking enzymatic activities.
source: We also found that they can be cleaved by human caspase-4 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, Figure 2C), but not by caspase-11/4 mutants lacking enzymatic activities.
evidence: Inferred from the statement that enzymatic activity is required for cleavage.

claim: The screening system for caspase-11 substrates is reliable.
source: These results indicate that our screening system is reliable.
evidence: Inferred from the validation of VgrG1a and VgrG2b as caspase-11 substrates.

claim: Caspase-11 has a particularly narrow substrate spectrum.
source: The number of target genes screened was very limited, which was consistent with the particularly narrow substrate spectrum of caspae-11 (Shi et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shi et al., 2023.

claim: Neither mouse caspase-11 nor human caspase-4 can cleave other members of the VgrG family (besides VgrG1a and VgrG2b).
source: We also tested other members of the VgrG family and found that neither mouse caspase-11 nor human caspase-4 could cleave these members (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–L).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–L.

claim: VgrG1a belongs to the H1-T6SS secretion system.
source: VgrG1a and VgrG2b belong to the secretion systems of H1-T6SS and H2-T6SS, and H1-T6SS does not have an effect on eukaryotic cells (Hood et al., 2010; Sana et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hood et al., 2010 and Sana et al., 2015.

claim: VgrG2b belongs to the H2-T6SS secretion system.
source: VgrG1a and VgrG2b belong to the secretion systems of H1-T6SS and H2-T6SS, and H1-T6SS does not have an effect on eukaryotic cells (Hood et al., 2010; Sana et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hood et al., 2010 and Sana et al., 2015.

claim: H1-T6SS does not have an effect on eukaryotic cells.
source: VgrG1a and VgrG2b belong to the secretion systems of H1-T6SS and H2-T6SS, and H1-T6SS does not have an effect on eukaryotic cells (Hood et al., 2010; Sana et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hood et al., 2010 and Sana et al., 2015.

claim: VgrG2b protein appears in macrophages after co-culturing P. aeruginosa with BMDM cells.
source: We found that after co-culturing of P. aeruginosa with BMDM cells, the VgrG2b protein appeared in macrophages (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 2D.

claim: Bacterial proteins are present in macrophages after co-incubation with P. aeruginosa.
source: Immunofluorescence experiments also showed the presence of bacterial proteins in macrophages after co-incubation with P. aeruginosa (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2E.

claim: VgrG2b is cleaved in wild-type BMDM cells after P. aeruginosa incubation.
source: We then incubated P. aeruginosa with wild-type BMDM cells and found that VgrG2b was cleaved in macrophages, while the cleavage band of VgrG2b disappeared in Casp11–/– BMDM cells (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 2F.

claim: The cleavage band of VgrG2b disappears in Casp11–/– BMDM cells after P. aeruginosa incubation.
source: We then incubated P. aeruginosa with wild-type BMDM cells and found that VgrG2b was cleaved in macrophages, while the cleavage band of VgrG2b disappeared in Casp11–/– BMDM cells (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 2F.

claim: The presence of caspase-11 induces VgrG2b cleavage in Casp11–/– BMDM cells.
source: We restored caspase-11 expression in Casp11–/– BMDM cells and found that the presence of caspase-11 induced VgrG2b cleavage (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 2G.

claim: Mutant caspase-11 cannot induce VgrG2b cleavage.
source: We also rescued Casp11–/– BMDM cells with wild-type and enzymatic mutant caspase-11 and found that mutant caspase-11 could not induce VgrG2b cleavage (Figure 2H).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 2H.

claim: VgrG2b is cleaved in human macrophages after P. aeruginosa incubation.
source: In addition, we incubated human macrophages with P. aeruginosa. As expected, VgrG2b was cleaved in human cells (Figure 2I).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 2I.

claim: P. aeruginosa lacking VgrG2b no longer inhibits the NLRP3 inflammasome.
source: We found that P. aeruginosa lacking VgrG2b no longer inhibited the NLRP3 inflammasome (Figure 2J, Figure 2—figure supplement 1M) and IL-1β could be secreted normally in the mutant bacteria-treated cells (Figure 2K).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 2J and Figure 2—figure supplement 1M.

claim: IL-1β can be secreted normally in cells treated with VgrG2b-deficient P. aeruginosa.
source: We found that P. aeruginosa lacking VgrG2b no longer inhibited the NLRP3 inflammasome (Figure 2J, Figure 2—figure supplement 1M) and IL-1β could be secreted normally in the mutant bacteria-treated cells (Figure 2K).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data in Figure 2K.

claim: H2-T6SS plays an important role in inhibiting host immune response through VgrG2b during P. aeruginosa infection.
source: These data indicate that H2-T6SS plays an important role in inhibiting host immune response through VgrG2b during P. aeruginosa infection, primarily targeting NLRP3 inflammasome activation rather than caspase-11 activation and GSDMD cleavage.
evidence: Inferred from the combined observations that VgrG2b deficiency relieves NLRP3 inhibition without affecting caspase-11 or GSDMD.

claim: H2-T6SS primarily targets NLRP3 inflammasome activation rather than caspase-11 activation and GSDMD cleavage.
source: These data indicate that H2-T6SS plays an important role in inhibiting host immune response through VgrG2b during P. aeruginosa infection, primarily targeting NLRP3 inflammasome activation rather than caspase-11 activation and GSDMD cleavage.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that VgrG2b affects NLRP3 but not upstream caspase-11/GSDMD signaling.

claim: Caspase-11 recognizes its substrate through a tertiary structure formed by its p22/p10 fragments.
source: Caspase-11 recognizes its substrate through a tertiary structure formed by its p22/p10 fragments (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2020.

claim: VgrG2b binds to the p22/p10 complex of enzymatically inactive mutant caspase-11.
source: Co-immunoprecipitation results showed that VgrG2b bound to the p22/p10 complex (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 3A.

claim: VgrG2b binds to the p22/p10 complex of mutant human caspase-4.
source: VgrG2b also bound to the p22/p10 complex of mutant human caspase-4 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: VgrG2b can be recognized by caspase-11/4.
source: These results suggest that VgrG2b can indeed be recognized by caspase-11/4.
evidence: Inferred from the binding data between VgrG2b and caspase-11/4 p22/p10 complexes.

claim: The cleavage site of VgrG2b by caspase-11 is at its C-terminus.
source: Based on the size of the cleaved VgrG2b fragment, we speculated that the cleavage site should be at its C-terminus.
evidence: Inferred from the size of the cleaved fragment observed in immunoblots.

claim: Only the D883A mutant of VgrG2b is no longer cleaved by caspase-11.
source: We constructed mutant plasmids carrying aspartic acid substitutions for VgrG2b and found that only the D883A mutant was no longer cleaved by caspase-11 (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 3B.

claim: The VgrG2b D883A mutant cannot be cleaved by human caspase-4.
source: We also verified that this VgrG2b mutant could not be cleaved by human caspase-4 (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 3C.

claim: A chimeric protein containing VgrG2a N-terminus, a linker sequence around D883 and VgrG2b C-terminus can be cleaved by caspase-11.
source: This chimeric protein could be cleaved by caspase-11 (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 3D.

claim: A chimeric protein containing VgrG2b N-terminus, a linker sequence around D883 and GFP cannot be cleaved by caspase-11.
source: Another chimeric protein containing VgrG2b N-terminus, a linker sequence around D883 and GFP cannot be cleaved by caspase-11 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The VgrG2b C-terminus is the site where VgrG2b binds to caspase-11.
source: Based on the substrate cleavage characteristic of caspase-11 that it needs to bind the target first to mediate cleavage (Wang et al., 2020), we speculated that the VgrG2b C-terminus was the site where VgrG2b bound to caspase-11.
evidence: Inferred from the known mechanism of caspase-11 substrate recognition and cleavage.

claim: The C-terminus of VgrG2b binds to the p22/p10 complex of caspase-11.
source: Indeed, the C-terminus of VgrG2b bound to the p22/p10 complex (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 3E.

claim: VgrG2b C-terminus binds to p22/p10 of human caspase-4.
source: Similarly, VgrG2b C-terminus also bound to p22/p10 of human caspase-4 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Caspase-11 induces the cleavage of recombinant VgrG2b.
source: We found that caspase-11 induced the cleavage of the recombinant VgrG2b (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by in vitro cleavage assay data in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Mutant VgrG2b (D883A) does not undergo cleavage after incubation with mouse BMDM.
source: After incubating this bacterium with mouse BMDM, mutant VgrG2b did not undergo cleavage (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 3G.

claim: The NLRP3 inflammasome is no longer inhibited after incubation with P. aeruginosa carrying the VgrG2b D883A mutation.
source: Consistently, the NLRP3 inflammasome was no longer inhibited (Figure 3H, I) and the secretion of IL-1β was restored post incubation with this P. aeruginosa mutant (Figure 3J), indicating that VgrG2b cleavage by caspase-11 is crucial for NLRP3 inhibition.
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 3H and quantification in Figure 3I.

claim: IL-1β secretion is restored after incubation with P. aeruginosa carrying the VgrG2b D883A mutation.
source: Consistently, the NLRP3 inflammasome was no longer inhibited (Figure 3H, I) and the secretion of IL-1β was restored post incubation with this P. aeruginosa mutant (Figure 3J), indicating that VgrG2b cleavage by caspase-11 is crucial for NLRP3 inhibition.
evidence: Supported by ELISA data in Figure 3J.

claim: VgrG2b cleavage by caspase-11 is crucial for NLRP3 inhibition.
source: Consistently, the NLRP3 inflammasome was no longer inhibited (Figure 3H, I) and the secretion of IL-1β was restored post incubation with this P. aeruginosa mutant (Figure 3J), indicating that VgrG2b cleavage by caspase-11 is crucial for NLRP3 inhibition.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that preventing VgrG2b cleavage (D883A mutation) relieves NLRP3 inhibition.

claim: Inhibition of caspase-11 blocks VgrG2b cleavage.
source: Moreover, inhibition of caspase-11 but not caspase-3 or -7 blocked VgrG2b cleavage (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Inhibition of caspase-3 or -7 does not block VgrG2b cleavage.
source: Moreover, inhibition of caspase-11 but not caspase-3 or -7 blocked VgrG2b cleavage (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The NLRP3 inflammasome is not suppressed after incubation of P. aeruginosa D883A mutant with human macrophages.
source: Similarly, after incubation of the P. aeruginosa mutant with human macrophages, the NLRP3 inflammasome was not suppressed (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G, H) and IL-1β was secreted normally (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G and quantification in 1H.

claim: IL-1β is secreted normally in human macrophages after incubation with P. aeruginosa D883A mutant.
source: Similarly, after incubation of the P. aeruginosa mutant with human macrophages, the NLRP3 inflammasome was not suppressed (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G, H) and IL-1β was secreted normally (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1I.

claim: VgrG2b cleavage at its C-terminus is crucial for NLRP3 inhibition.
source: These results indicate that VgrG2b cleavage at its C-terminus is crucial for NLRP3 inhibition.
evidence: Inferred from the combined observations that D883A mutation prevents cleavage and relieves NLRP3 inhibition.

claim: NLRP3 fragments repeatedly appeared in positive clones from yeast two-hybrid screening using VgrG2b C-terminus as bait.
source: In the positive clones obtained from the screening, the NLRP3 fragments repeatedly appeared (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by yeast two-hybrid screening data in Figure 4A.

claim: VgrG2b C-terminus binds to NLRP3 in HEK293T cells.
source: We validated their interaction in HEK293T cells and found that VgrG2b C-terminus indeed bound to NLRP3 (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4B.

claim: Full-length VgrG2b binds to NLRP3.
source: Full-length VgrG2b also bound to NLRP3 (Figure 4C), but the N-terminus of VgrG2b did not bind to NLRP3 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4C.

claim: The N-terminus of VgrG2b does not bind to NLRP3.
source: Full-length VgrG2b also bound to NLRP3 (Figure 4C), but the N-terminus of VgrG2b did not bind to NLRP3 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: VgrG2b C-terminus interacts with endogenous NLRP3 in BMDM cells.
source: VgrG2b C-terminus was introduced into BMDM cells through cell-penetrating peptides, and it was found that the C-terminus interacted with endogenous NLRP3 (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4D.

claim: VgrG2b C-terminus interacts with human NLRP3.
source: Similarly, VgrG2b C-terminus also interacted with the human NLRP3 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: NLRP3 interacts with the C-terminus of VgrG2b rather than the full-length VgrG2b after P. aeruginosa incubation with mouse BMDM cells.
source: In addition, we incubated P. aeruginosa with mouse BMDM cells and found that NLRP3 interacted with the C-terminus of VgrG2b rather than the full-length one (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4E.

claim: NLRP3 binds to the C-terminus of VgrG2b after P. aeruginosa incubation with human macrophages.
source: The same result was observed after incubation of P. aeruginosa with human macrophages, where NLRP3 bound to the C-terminus of VgrG2b (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: VgrG2b C-terminus colocalizes with NLRP3 inside BMDM cells.
source: The colocalization between VgrG2b C-terminus and NLRP3 was observed inside BMDM cells (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 4F.

claim: VgrG2b C-terminus does not bind to mouse GSDMD.
source: The VgrG2b C-terminus did not bind to mouse GSDMD (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), ASC (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E), nor caspase-1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F, G), indicating that the binding targets of VgrG2b in host cells is very specific.
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: VgrG2b C-terminus does not bind to ASC.
source: The VgrG2b C-terminus did not bind to mouse GSDMD (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), ASC (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E), nor caspase-1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F, G), indicating that the binding targets of VgrG2b in host cells is very specific.
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: VgrG2b C-terminus does not bind to caspase-1.
source: The VgrG2b C-terminus did not bind to mouse GSDMD (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), ASC (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E), nor caspase-1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F, G), indicating that the binding targets of VgrG2b in host cells is very specific.
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F, G.

claim: The binding targets of VgrG2b in host cells are very specific.
source: The VgrG2b C-terminus did not bind to mouse GSDMD (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), ASC (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E), nor caspase-1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F, G), indicating that the binding targets of VgrG2b in host cells is very specific.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that VgrG2b-C binds NLRP3 but not other inflammasome components.

claim: The interaction area between VgrG2b C-terminus and NLRP3 is at the NACHT–LRR junction of NLRP3.
source: We further searched for the region where VgrG2b C-terminus interacted with NLRP3 (Figure 4G), and found that their interaction area was at the NACHT–LRR junction of NLRP3 (Figure 4H, I).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data with NLRP3 truncations in Figure 4H, I.

claim: VgrG2b cannot be cleaved and does not bind to NLRP3 in Casp11 knockout BMDM cells.
source: In Casp11 knockout BMDM cells, VgrG2b could not be cleaved and did not bind to NLRP3 (Figure 4J).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4J.

claim: VgrG2b still undergoes cleavage and binds to NLRP3 in Gsdmd knockout cells.
source: However, in Gsdmd knockout cells, VgrG2b still underwent cleavage and bound to NLRP3 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1H.

claim: The NLRP3 inflammasome is not activated in the absence of GSDMD.
source: In the absence of GSDMD, the NLRP3 inflammasome was not activated (Broz et al., 2020; Kayagaki et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Broz et al., 2020 and Kayagaki et al., 2015.

claim: The binding of VgrG2b C-terminus to NLRP3 is independent of NLRP3 activation.
source: This result indicates that the binding of VgrG2b C-terminus to NLRP3 is independent of NLRP3 activation, but requires a cleaved segment of VgrG2b processed by caspase-11.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that VgrG2b-C binds NLRP3 in Gsdmd knockout cells where NLRP3 is not activated.

claim: The binding of VgrG2b C-terminus to NLRP3 requires a cleaved segment of VgrG2b processed by caspase-11.
source: This result indicates that the binding of VgrG2b C-terminus to NLRP3 is independent of NLRP3 activation, but requires a cleaved segment of VgrG2b processed by caspase-11.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that VgrG2b does not bind NLRP3 in Casp11 knockout cells.

claim: VgrG2b possesses a metalloprotease activity.
source: VgrG2b also possesses a metalloprotease activity (Wood et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wood et al., 2019.

claim: Mutating VgrG2b to disable its protease activity does not prohibit caspase-11 cleavage on VgrG2b.
source: To test whether its protease activity is responsible for VgrG2b cleavage observed in our study, we mutated VgrG2b to disable its protease activity and found that this mutant form did not prohibit caspase-11 cleavage on VgrG2b (Figure 4—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1I.

claim: VgrG2b mutant C-terminus binds NLRP3 just like its wild-type counterpart.
source: Moreover, VgrG2b mutant C-terminus bound NLRP3 and inhibited NLRP3 activation just like its wild-type counterpart (Figure 4—figure supplement 1J and K).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1J and immunoblotting in 1K.

claim: VgrG2b mutant C-terminus inhibits NLRP3 activation just like its wild-type counterpart.
source: Moreover, VgrG2b mutant C-terminus bound NLRP3 and inhibited NLRP3 activation just like its wild-type counterpart (Figure 4—figure supplement 1J and K).
